## Could this result arise if there were no effect? {#could-this-arise .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Predict before the reveal</p>
<p class="medium">We observed a mean paired change of <strong>−10.4 U/mg</strong>.</p>
<p class="takeaway">What would we expect if the true average treatment effect were exactly zero?</p>
<div class="fragment keyline"><p class="medium">Same variability. Six new preparations.<br>Same paired experiment. True mean <strong>0</strong>.</p></div>
<p class="fine">Hypothetical L1 model: no average effect, not identical responses in every preparation.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 02:56–02:58 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Reconnect to the unanswered question. Invite predictions before the reveal. Keep the six observed differences and −10.4 estimate unchanged. Change only the mean effect in the simulation from −14 to zero. Biological effect SD remains 9, tube SD 3 and technical-reading SD 2.5; pairing, triplicate averaging and assay rounding remain. Positive and negative preparation effects can still occur. Do not name the null hypothesis yet. This is a hypothetical generating model, not a conclusion about compound Q.

**Conceptual point:** The no-average-effect situation is a concrete model for repeated experiments.

**Likely misconception:** No average effect means every preparation has zero response or no measurement variation.

**Optional follow-up:** Would all six changes be zero in every repetition?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 89–99, 106–114, 136, 142–146; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 50–55; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 30–39. Figures rebuilt; chance-language corrections follow CONTENT_MAP.md. R stats documentation, Student t distribution: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/TDist.html. The paired t calculation uses the six differences. Interpretation reference: ASA statement, https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf.

:::

## Zero on average does not mean zero every time {#zero-not-every-time}

<img class="data-plot" src="figures/generated/null-three-repeats.png" alt="First three simulated no-average-effect experiments, each with six paired changes and its own mean." />
<p class="takeaway">Different sample means, even when the true mean is zero</p>
<p class="fine">Dark dots: preparation changes. Rust diamonds: means. Vertical line: fixed true mean 0.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 02:58–03:00 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Trace the six dots and the diamond in each row. These are the first three repetitions from seed 20261006, not selected examples. New preparations give nonzero means despite a fixed population average of zero. Use the same within-tube averaging and Q-minus-vehicle subtraction as for our observed experiment. The fixed line belongs to the hypothetical model; the diamonds belong to particular samples.

**Conceptual point:** Nonzero estimates are expected under repeated sampling even without an average treatment effect.

**Likely misconception:** Any nonzero observed average contradicts a zero-average model.

**Optional follow-up:** Which feature changes between rows, and which remains fixed?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 89–99, 106–114, 136, 142–146; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 50–55; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 30–39. The paired t calculation uses the six differences. Interpretation reference: ASA statement, https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf.

## What would the no-effect model produce? {#build-null-distribution}

<div class="uncertainty-stack">
<img data-fragment-index="0" class="data-plot fragment fade-out" src="figures/generated/null-means-10.png" alt="Means from the first ten null experiments." />
<img data-fragment-index="0" class="data-plot fragment fade-in-then-out" src="figures/generated/null-means-100.png" alt="Means from the first hundred null experiments." />
<img data-fragment-index="1" class="data-plot fragment" src="figures/generated/null-means-10000.png" alt="Means from ten thousand no-average-effect experiments." />
</div>
<p class="takeaway fragment" data-fragment-index="2">The <strong>null distribution</strong> · H<sub>0</sub>: mean paired effect = 0</p>
<p class="fine">One entry = one experiment’s mean. Six new paired changes per experiment.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 03:00–03:03 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Accumulate 10, 100 and 10,000 means before naming the distribution on a final click. Define a null distribution as the distribution of the statistic across repeated experiments if the null hypothesis and model assumptions were true. Then name H0: the population mean paired effect is zero. The horizontal axis is in the same units, with the same 36-unit span and one-unit bins as the previous sampling-distribution sequence, now centered on zero. It is not a histogram of six observations and not a distribution of probabilities that hypotheses are true.

**Conceptual point:** The null distribution is the earlier sampling-distribution idea evaluated under a specified null model.

**Likely misconception:** H0 has been established by simulating from it, or each bar represents a different possible hypothesis.

**Optional follow-up:** What assumption produced the center of this histogram?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 89–99, 106–114, 136, 142–146; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 50–55; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 30–39. Figures rebuilt; chance-language corrections follow CONTENT_MAP.md. R stats documentation, Student t distribution: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/TDist.html. The paired t calculation uses the six differences. Interpretation reference: ASA statement, https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf.

:::

## Does our observed mean look ordinary here? {#observed-in-null .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Ordinary or unusual? · look before reading on</p>
<img class="data-plot" src="figures/generated/null-observed-mean.png" alt="Null distribution of means with observed mean minus 10.4 marked in rust." />
<p class="takeaway">Ordinary or unusual under this no-average-effect model?</p>
<p class="fine">Same null simulation and axes. Observed data remain unchanged.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 03:03–03:05 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Allow a short visual judgment before introducing any probability. The observed mean is toward the left of the simulated cloud. Ask what controls its distance from the center relative to the cloud’s width. Do not quote the fraction of raw means beyond this line as the paired t p-value. This raw-mean simulation uses a known generating spread; the real analysis estimates spread from six differences. The next slides make that transition explicit. No probabilities of hypotheses are being shown.

**Conceptual point:** An estimate is evaluated relative to what its reference model would produce.

**Likely misconception:** A visually distant mean is enough by itself to provide a calibrated p-value when the variability is unknown.

**Optional follow-up:** Could the same −10.4 be more ordinary in a noisier experiment?

:::

## Is −10.4 equally surprising in every experiment? {#raw-mean-needs-scale}

<img class="data-plot short-plot" src="figures/generated/null-same-mean.png" alt="Two hypothetical estimates both minus 10.4, with one-SE spans of 2 and 10 U/mg." />
<p class="takeaway">The distance from zero needs a scale.</p>
<p class="fine">Constructed comparison. Lines show ±1 estimated SE, not confidence intervals or a recommended generic error-bar display.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 03:05–03:07 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Compare the identical estimates with estimated SEs of 2 and 10. These are constructed illustrations, not alternative analyses of our six observations. The same raw mean is many SEs from zero in one and about one SE from zero in the other. The short lines are explicitly one-SE spans used to explain standardization; do not teach them as a replacement for raw data or confidence intervals. Keep magnitude distinct from extremeness relative to uncertainty.

**Conceptual point:** The raw mean alone cannot specify how unusual an estimate is under a null model.

**Likely misconception:** A p-value is an effect size, or the same numerical effect must always give the same p-value.

**Optional follow-up:** Which scenario puts the estimate further from zero in units of its uncertainty?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 89–99, 106–114, 136, 142–146; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 50–55; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 30–39. The paired t calculation uses the six differences. Interpretation reference: ASA statement, https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf.

:::

## How many standard errors away from zero? {#our-paired-t}

<img class="data-plot short-plot" src="figures/generated/null-se-steps.png" alt="Observed mean minus 10.4 and null zero, separated by about 2.10 steps of the estimated SE 4.96." />
<p class="takeaway">Our mean sits 2.1 SE steps below zero.</p>
<p class="medium">This distance, counted in SE steps, is called <strong>t</strong>. Here t = −2.10.</p>
<p class="small">Now we ask: how often would chance alone produce a result at least that far from zero?</p>

::: notes
**Time: 03:07–03:10 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Point to the figure. Zero is where no effect would sit. Our mean is 2.1 SE steps below it. That gap is what we need to judge — not the raw number, but how far it sits relative to the uncertainty in our estimate. Name it once: this SE-step distance is the t statistic, t = −2.10; it is the number software reports and the one you will see in papers. Negative means lower activity with Q; we will count distance in either direction. The question now is how often the null model would produce a result at least this far from zero. That is what the next slide answers.

**Conceptual point:** The standardized distance from zero is what the reference distribution compares against, not the raw mean.

**Likely misconception:** The test uses the SD of 36 technical readings, or a bigger raw mean always gives a smaller p-value regardless of SE.

**Optional follow-up:** If our SE had been 10 instead of 5, how many steps away would our mean be?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 89–99, 106–114, 136, 142–146; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 50–55; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 30–39.

:::

## How often would a result be at least this extreme? {#two-sided-p-value}

<img class="data-plot null-tail-plot" src="figures/generated/null-two-tails.png" alt="t distribution with both tails shaded beyond minus 2.10 and plus 2.10." />
<p class="null-definition">The p-value: if there were no true effect, how often would an experiment land at least as far from zero as ours — 2.1 SE steps, in either direction?</p>
<p class="takeaway fragment"><strong>Two-sided p = 0.090</strong> · both directions count</p>

::: notes
**Time: 03:10–03:13 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Point to the observed t at −2.10 and the equally distant +2.10 boundary. The question was about an average change in either direction, so add both tail probabilities. The actual paired t p-value is 0.08987058, rounded to 0.090. Under H0 and the assumptions, about 9% of repeated experiments produce absolute t at least 2.10. The simulation gives 9.07%, close to the analytical value; it is the standardized statistic, not the raw mean, being counted. Integrating the t distribution includes its entire infinite tails even though the plot shows only −5 to +5. Do not choose the direction after seeing a negative estimate.

**Conceptual point:** A p-value is a tail probability conditional on the null and statistical assumptions.

**Likely misconception:** The shaded area is the probability that H0 is true, or refers only to exactly the observed statistic.

**Optional follow-up:** Why does the right tail count when our observed estimate is negative?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 89–99, 106–114, 136, 142–146; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 50–55; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 30–39. Figures rebuilt; chance-language corrections follow CONTENT_MAP.md. R stats documentation, Student t distribution: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/TDist.html. The paired t calculation uses the six differences. Interpretation reference: ASA statement, https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf.

:::

## What does p = 0.090 mean? {#interpret-p-value .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Which statements are correct?</p>
<div class="null-options"><p>A · There is a 9% probability that H<sub>0</sub> is true.</p><p>B · There is a 9% probability that the result occurred by chance.</p><p>C · There is a 91% probability that the treatment really works.</p><p>D · A large p-value proves there is no effect.</p></div>
<div class="fragment"><p class="takeaway"><strong>All four are incorrect.</strong></p><p class="small">If there were no true effect, about 9% of repeated experiments would land at least 2.1 SE steps from zero.</p></div>
<p class="small fragment">B is close — but drops the condition. Repair: <em>"Assuming no true average effect, about 9% of repetitions produce a result at least this extreme."</em> Without that phrase, B implies the p-value assigns probability to H<sub>0</sub> being false — which it cannot do.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 03:13–03:17 (4 minutes).**

**Say:** Give one minute of individual choice and a minute of pair discussion, then reveal and debrief. All options reverse or distort the conditional statement. We assumed H0 to calculate the reference distribution; we did not calculate its probability. One minus p is not a probability that a compound works, and a large p does not prove zero effect.

On B specifically: it is the most seductive wrong answer and worth one extra minute. “By chance” sounds like it means “no real effect,” but that is exactly what we have not established. Results arise from random sampling whether or not there is a true effect — the question is only how often they are this extreme under H0. B drops the conditioning phrase, so it reads as if the p-value assigns a 9% probability to the null being true and a 91% probability to the treatment working — which is option C restated. Once participants add “assuming no true average effect,” B becomes approximately the correct statement. That addition is the whole point: the condition is not decorative, it is what makes the number mean anything.

**Conceptual point:** The probability is about possible data/statistics under an assumed model, not about the truth of that model.

**Likely misconception:** Subtracting p from one gives confidence that the treatment works.

**Optional follow-up:** Which phrase must appear before “about 9% of repeated experiments”?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 89–99, 106–114, 136, 142–146; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 50–55; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 30–39. Figures rebuilt; chance-language corrections follow CONTENT_MAP.md. R stats documentation, Student t distribution: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/TDist.html. The paired t calculation uses the six differences. Interpretation reference: ASA statement, https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf.

:::

## How does this connect to our interval? {#p-and-ci}

<img class="data-plot short-plot" src="figures/generated/null-ci-zero.png" alt="Observed mean and 95 percent paired t confidence interval, with null zero inside the interval." />
<p class="takeaway">95% CI: <strong>−23.2 to +2.3</strong> · p = <strong>0.090</strong></p>
<div class="fragment"><p class="small">For the matching two-sided paired t procedure:<br>95% CI excludes 0 ⇔ p &lt; 0.05<br>95% CI includes 0 ⇔ p ≥ 0.05</p></div>
<p class="fine">The interval also shows the size and uncertainty of the effect.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 03:17–03:20 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Return to the unchanged interval and its zero line. At the conventional 0.05 threshold, the matching two-sided paired t calculation and its 95% interval agree as displayed. Includes means including the endpoints; at an exact endpoint the matching p is 0.05. This correspondence requires the same data, assumptions, contrast and procedure. It is not a general rule about overlap of two separate group intervals. The interval gives the range and magnitude of compatible mean effects, rather than compatibility with only the single zero value. Here it permits appreciable reductions as well as near-zero and small positive effects. The threshold’s decision meaning comes next.

**Conceptual point:** The p-value and corresponding confidence interval are linked views, while the interval retains magnitude and uncertainty.

**Likely misconception:** An interval containing zero proves zero effect, or overlap of group intervals is the relevant rule.

**Optional follow-up:** What information would we lose by reporting only p = 0.090?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 89–99, 106–114, 136, 142–146; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 50–55; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 30–39. Figures rebuilt; chance-language corrections follow CONTENT_MAP.md. R stats documentation, Student t distribution: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/TDist.html. The paired t calculation uses the six differences. Interpretation reference: ASA statement, https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf.

:::

## What does a 0.05 decision rule control? {#alpha-type-one}

<p class="medium">Pre-specify α = 0.05.<br>Reject H<sub>0</sub> when p &lt; 0.05.</p>
<img class="data-plot null-decision-plot" src="figures/generated/null-decisions.png" alt="First hundred null-model experiments shown as decisions; rust crosses reject the true null, teal dots do not." />
<div class="fragment"><p class="takeaway"><strong>Type I error:</strong> rejecting H<sub>0</sub> when H<sub>0</sub> is true</p><p class="small">About 5% in repeated use under H<sub>0</sub> and the model.</p></div>
<p class="fine">First 100 null repetitions, in order. Rust crosses: p &lt; 0.05. Across 10,000: 4.98%.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 03:20–03:23 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Only now introduce alpha as the prespecified decision threshold, a convention rather than a natural evidence boundary. A rejection under the chosen rule is often called statistically significant; that label does not establish biological importance. Every displayed experiment was generated with a true zero mean. Each rust cross is a rejection of a true H0, called a Type I error. There are not necessarily exactly five crosses in each block of 100; the first 100 are shown unselected. Across the same 10,000 null experiments 4.98% meet p<0.05. Under the ideal continuous normal model this rule’s long-run Type I rate is 5%; our rounded simulation approximates it. Alpha is not the probability that a particular conclusion is wrong, nor the proportion of all rejected claims that are false. A testing rule must be fixed in advance; do not retune it for the observed result.

**Conceptual point:** Alpha calibrates a repeated-use decision rule conditional on a true null, rather than labeling a universal evidence boundary.

**Likely misconception:** Every result with p<0.05 has a 5% probability of being a false finding.

**Optional follow-up:** Why can one hundred experiments show something other than exactly five crosses?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 89–99, 106–114, 136, 142–146; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 50–55; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 30–39. Figures rebuilt; chance-language corrections follow CONTENT_MAP.md. R stats documentation, Student t distribution: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/TDist.html. The paired t calculation uses the six differences. Interpretation reference: ASA statement, https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf.

:::

## Are these scientifically different? {#threshold-neighbours .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Two hypothetical results</p>
<div class="null-neighbours"><p>p = 0.049</p><p>p = 0.051</p></div>
<p class="takeaway fragment">A decision threshold does not create a jump in evidence.</p>
<p class="small">“Significant” and “not significant” cannot replace effect size, uncertainty or biological importance.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 03:23–03:25 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Ask whether these values alone make the studies scientifically different. Under a prespecified p<0.05 rule the labels differ, but the data’s incompatibility with the null changes continuously rather than jumping at the cutoff. The comparison is only about nearby values for comparable analyses; p-values alone cannot rank very different experiments or scientific importance. A statistically significant result can be biologically small and does not guarantee replication. A result just above the convention does not establish no effect. Ask for estimates, intervals, design and biological context.

**Conceptual point:** A continuous compatibility summary and a threshold-based decision are different things.

**Likely misconception:** The p=0.049 study has discovered a real important effect and the p=0.051 study has found none.

**Optional follow-up:** What would you request before deciding which result matters biologically?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 89–99, 106–114, 136, 142–146; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 50–55; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 30–39. Figures rebuilt; chance-language corrections follow CONTENT_MAP.md. R stats documentation, Student t distribution: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/TDist.html. The paired t calculation uses the six differences. Interpretation reference: ASA statement, https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf.

:::

## What can we report about compound Q? {#report-q-with-p .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Report to a neighbour · 1 minute</p>
<img class="data-plot short-plot" src="figures/generated/null-ci-zero.png" alt="The same L1 paired-effect interval from minus 23.2 to plus 2.3 around mean minus 10.4." />
<p class="takeaway"><strong>−10.4 U/mg</strong> · 95% CI <strong>−23.2 to +2.3</strong><br>paired t-test: t = <strong>−2.10</strong> · two-sided p = <strong>0.090</strong></p>
<p class="small">What did we observe? How large and how uncertain?<br>How compatible with zero? What can we not conclude?</p>
<p class="fine">Six L1 preparation pairs · conditional on independent, approximately normal differences.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 03:25–03:28 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Give a minute for a spoken or written report and two for debrief. The observed mean is a reduction of 10.4 U/mg, with the displayed broad interval. The t statistic is 2.10 estimated SEs below zero. Assuming zero mean and the model, an absolute statistic this large or larger occurs about 9% of the time. At a prespecified 0.05 rule this would not reject H0; explain if using that phrase that it does not establish H0. The interval remains compatible with substantial reductions and some small increases. No validated biological relevance threshold is supplied. Do not conclude that Q works or does not work, infer a mechanism, or generalize beyond the specified L1 process. Dependence or bias would undermine the simple model rather than being repaired by a p-value.

**Conceptual point:** A result needs the estimated effect, uncertainty, conditional model comparison and bounded claim together.

**Likely misconception:** p>0.05 proves no effect, or the estimate and interval can be omitted once p is known.

**Optional follow-up:** What claim does this experiment permit, and which statement would still be too strong?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 89–99, 106–114, 136, 142–146; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 50–55; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 30–39. Figures rebuilt; chance-language corrections follow CONTENT_MAP.md. R stats documentation, Student t distribution: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/TDist.html. The paired t calculation uses the six differences. Interpretation reference: ASA statement, https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf.

:::

## One question to carry forward {#too-small-bridge}

<p class="quote uncertainty-final">What if the experiment was simply too small to give a clear answer?</p>

::: notes
**Time: 03:28–03:29 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Read the question and stop. It is a possibility to investigate, not a conclusion that this experiment was necessarily too small. Leave the question unanswered. Do not introduce the next block’s concepts, formulas or planning advice.

**Conceptual point:** An unresolved result motivates a new question about the experiment’s ability to answer the biological question.

**Likely misconception:** The present result by itself establishes the reason for uncertainty or prescribes the next design.

**Optional follow-up:** No additional prompt: leave the question open.
